title: "Linking two feeds by co-location"

execute:

Positions of one vessel often come from several feeds that name it
differently: a national tracking unit, an AIS transponder's MMSI, a registry
number. Where the key between them is missing or doubtful, the tracks
themselves can supply it: two ids are one vessel when their pings move
together.
[rb_link_vessel_tracks()](../reference/rb_link_vessel_tracks.html) scores
every pair of ids for that, per month by default.

```{r}
library(ramb)
library(dplyr)
```

## A small example

The track of the Italian pot vessel shipped with ramb
([rb_read_example()](../reference/rb_read_example.html)) stands for a
tracking unit, `x`. A second feed, `y`, holds three ids: `A`, the same vessel
heard every three minutes and slightly off; `B`, a vessel steaming 800 m
abreast of it a minute behind (a pair trawler, a tender); and `C`, a vessel
that works the same ground a day later.

```{r}
x <- collect(rb_read_example("wkssfgeo2_it_pots")) |>
  transmute(unit = vid, time, lon, lat, speed)
three_min <- filter(x, as.numeric(time) %% 180 == 0)
y <- bind_rows(
  three_min |> mutate(id = "A", time = time + 15, lat = lat + 0.0003),
  x |> mutate(id = "B", time = time + 60, lat = lat + 800 / 111195),
  x |> mutate(id = "C", time = time + 86400)
) |>
  select(id, time, lon, lat, speed)
```

## The scores

A hit is a moving ping of the unit with a moving ping of the other id within
5 minutes and 2 km. The opportunity is the unit's moving pings with any ping
of that id within 5 minutes, wherever it is. Dividing by the opportunity
keeps a sparse feed such as `A` from looking like a poor match.

```{r}
links <- rb_link_vessel_tracks(x, y, id_x = "unit", id_y = "id")
links |>
  select(unit, id, period, n_x, hits, opportunity, score, median_m, rank, id_other, score_other, strong) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)
```

`A` and `B` both score fully: co-location alone cannot tell a vessel from one
that keeps it company. The table keeps that ambiguity. Each row carries the best
other id and its score, so a link whose runner-up scores as high needs another
witness: a registry, the MMSI's call sign, the vessel's port calls. The median
distance of the hits differs (`A` a couple of hundred metres, `B` about 500 m;
it is measured to the nearest ping within the 5 minutes, so it holds the
vessel's own movement too), but it is a hint, not proof.

`C` works the same ground a day later, and the pot vessel goes back to the same
ground day after day, so `C` meets the unit on some of its later trips. It
scores in part and is not `strong`: a neighbour on the same ground, not the
same vessel.

The defaults (5 min, 2 km, 1 knot, and a month `strong` at 20 opportunities
and a score of 0.8) are the Icelandic calibration; a random other vessel
scored a hit there 2 in 100,000 times. Filter both feeds to the area and
years of interest first.
